questions.topic: Counting passwords; probability of at least one zero
questions.stem: A bank issues a unique six-digit password to each of its online customers. The password may contain any of the numbers 0 to 9 in any position and numbers may be repeated. For example, the following is a valid password.
questions.fig: Six boxes holding the example password 0 7 1 7 3 7. In part (c), a row of six boxes with a star (*) in three of them.

parts.q: How many different passwords are possible?
parts.scheme: $10^6 = 1\,000\,000$. Accept the correct answer without work. (Answers like $10.9.8.7.6.5 = 151\,200$ or $9^6$ get partial credit only.)

idea.title: The fundamental principle of counting
idea.text: If you make several choices one after another, multiply the number of options for each choice. 4 starters and 6 mains give 4 × 6 = 24 different pairs, because every starter can go with every main.

steps.say: Think of the password as six empty boxes. Each box can hold any digit from 0 to 9: that is 10 options. Digits can repeat, so every box still has all 10 options.
Multiply the options for the six boxes together (the fundamental principle of counting).
Work it out. So 1 000 000 different passwords are possible.

parts.tip: Repeats allowed means the number of options stays the same for every box.

parts.q: How many different passwords do not contain any zero?

steps.say: No zero allowed, so each box can only be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9. That is 9 options for every box.
Multiply the six 9s. So 531 441 passwords have no zero.

parts.q: One password is selected at random from all the possible passwords. What is the probability that this password contains at least one zero?

idea.title: "At least one" is everything except "none"
idea.text: A password either has no zeros or it has at least one zero. Those two groups make up all the passwords, so: at least one zero = total − no zeros. In probability: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

steps.say: Probability = the number of passwords you want ÷ the number of passwords there are. The total is from part (a): 1 000 000.
math: P = \frac{\text{passwords with at least one } 0}{\text{all passwords}}

steps.say: Counting "at least one zero" directly is hard. Instead, take the passwords with no zero (from (b)(i)) away from the total. Every password that is left has at least one zero.
Divide by the total. So the probability is 0.468559.

parts.tip: "At least one" questions: count "none" first, then subtract.

parts.q: John is issued with one such password from the bank. Each time John wants to access his account online, the bank’s website requires him to input three of his password digits into the boxes provided. For example, he may be asked for the 2nd, 4th and 5th digits, as shown below. In how many different ways can the bank select the three required boxes?

idea.title: When the order does not matter
idea.text: Here the bank only cares which 3 boxes, not the order it asks for them. So list each group of boxes once, always writing the box numbers from smallest to biggest.

steps.say: Number the boxes 1 to 6. The bank picks 3 different boxes. Asking for boxes 2, 4, 5 is the same as asking for 5, 2, 4, so write every choice with its numbers going up. Then no choice is counted twice.
Start with every choice that uses box 1. After the 1, pick the second box and then the third, always going up.
Next, the choices that start with box 2. (Choices with box 1 are all in the first list.)
Then the choices starting with 3, and the only one starting with 4.
Add them up. So the bank can select the three boxes in 20 different ways.

parts.tip: Shortcut: 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 ordered picks, but each group of 3 boxes is picked in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 different orders, so 120 ÷ 6 = 20.

questions.topic: Counting meal choices; probability with independent people

parts.q: A restaurant is offering a three-course meal consisting of one starter, one main course and one dessert. There are 4 different starters, 6 different main courses and 8 different desserts to choose from. How many different three-course meal combinations are available?
parts.scheme: $4 \times 6 \times 8 = 192$ available. Correct answer without supporting work: full credit.

idea.title: The fundamental principle of counting
idea.text: If you make several choices one after another, multiply the number of options for each choice. 4 starters and 6 mains give 4 × 6 = 24 different pairs, because every starter can go with every main.

steps.say: A meal is three choices made one after another: a starter, then a main course, then a dessert. Write down how many options each course has.
Every starter can go with every main, and every starter-and-main pair can go with every dessert. So multiply. There are 192 different three-course meals.

parts.tip: Multiply, don't add: 4 + 6 + 8 = 18 counts dishes, not meals.

parts.q: When Jack visits the restaurant he discovers that the restaurant still has the 4 starters and the 6 main courses available but is sold out of some of the desserts. Jack now has 120 different three-course meal combinations to choose from. How many different desserts are still available to Jack?

steps.say: Call the number of desserts left d. The counting rule still works: starters × mains × desserts = number of meals.
4 × 6 = 24, so 24 lots of d make 120.
Divide both sides by 24. So 5 desserts are still available.

parts.q: In a large population 1 in 8 of the people play tennis. Four people are chosen at random from the population. What is the probability that the fourth person chosen is the only one to play tennis?
parts.scheme: $\frac78 \times \frac78 \times \frac78 \times \frac18 = \frac{343}{4096}$ or $0{\cdot}08374$. ($\frac78 \times \frac78 \times \frac78 \times \frac18$ and stops: high partial credit.)

idea.title: Independent events: multiply
idea.text: If one result does not change the chances of the next, the chance of a whole list of results is the single chances multiplied together. And P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

steps.say: 1 in 8 play tennis, so P(plays) = 1/8. Everyone else doesn't: P(doesn't play) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.
"The fourth is the only one" means: 1st no, 2nd no, 3rd no, 4th yes. The question says which person plays, so there is only one order.
The people are independent, so multiply the four probabilities. The probability is 343/4096 ≈ 0.08374.

parts.q: Three people are chosen at random from the population. What is the probability that exactly two of them play tennis?

idea.title: "Exactly" means count the orders
idea.text: When the question doesn't say which people, the result can happen in different orders. Work out the probability of one order, then multiply by the number of orders.

steps.say: Exactly two play and one doesn't. The one who doesn't could be the 1st, the 2nd or the 3rd person, so there are 3 different orders.
Each order has the same probability: two lots of 1/8 and one 7/8.
There are 3 orders, so multiply by 3. The probability is 21/512 ≈ 0.04101.

parts.tip: Don't forget the × 3: any one of the three people could be the one who doesn't play.

questions.topic: Mean and median; counting choices of subjects
questions.fig: Part (b) shows a table of three groups of subjects: Group A (3 subjects): French, Spanish, German; Group B (4 subjects): Biology, Physics, Chemistry, Business; Group C (5 subjects): Art, Accounting, History, Geography, Home Economics.

parts.q: A list of 7 numbers is shown below. 17, 8, 9, 8, 14, 11, 28. Find the mean of these 7 numbers, correct to 1 decimal place.

idea.title: The mean
idea.text: The mean is the "fair share": add up all the numbers, then divide by how many numbers there are.

steps.say: Add up all 7 numbers.
Divide by how many numbers there are (7). Round to 1 decimal place: the next digit is 7, so round up. The mean is 13.6.

parts.q: Find the median of these 7 numbers.

idea.title: The median
idea.text: The median is the middle number once the list is in order. With an odd number of values there is one middle number; with an even number, it is halfway between the two middle numbers.

steps.say: Put the numbers in order from smallest to biggest.
There are 7 numbers, so the middle one is the 4th: (7 + 1) ÷ 2 = 4. The median is 11.

parts.q: One more number is added to the list. The new median is 10·5. Find the number that was added to the list.
parts.scheme: One new number means the median is the average of the two centre numbers: $\frac{10 + 11}{2} = 10{\cdot}5$, so the answer is 10.

steps.say: Now there are 8 numbers. With an even count, the median is halfway between the two middle numbers (the 4th and the 5th).
10.5 is between 9 and 11, so the new number x must sit between 9 and 11 in the list. Then the two middle numbers are x and 11.
Halfway between x and 11 is 10.5. Solve it. The number added was 10.

parts.tip: Check: 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 17, 28 has middle numbers 10 and 11, so the median is 10.5.

parts.q: Ben has to choose three subjects to study. He must pick one subject from each of these three groups: Group A (3 subjects), Group B (4 subjects), Group C (5 subjects). How many different choices of three subjects can Ben make, picking one from each group?
parts.scheme: $3 \times 4 \times 5 = 60$, or list some or all choices and count them. Correct answer without work: full credit. (Treating it as $3 + 4 + 5$ gets partial credit only.)

idea.title: The fundamental principle of counting
idea.text: If you make several choices one after another, multiply the number of options for each choice. 4 starters and 6 mains give 4 × 6 = 24 different pairs, because every starter can go with every main.

steps.say: Ben makes three choices one after another: one subject from A (3 options), one from B (4 options) and one from C (5 options).
Every choice from A can go with every choice from B and every choice from C, so multiply. Ben can make 60 different choices.

parts.tip: Multiply, don't add: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 is the number of subjects, not the number of choices.

parts.q: The school is going to add one extra subject to one of these groups (A, B, or C). Which group should the extra subject be added to, in order to make the number of different choices of three subjects that Ben can make as large as possible? Justify your answer.
parts.scheme: Group A. Extra A: $4 \times 4 \times 5 = 80$; extra B: $3 \times 5 \times 5 = 75$; extra C: $3 \times 4 \times 6 = 72$. Or: the biggest pair is $4 \times 5$ (B and C), so the biggest increase comes from increasing A. (Group A with no justification: low partial credit.)

steps.say: Try each group in turn: add 1 to that group's number of subjects and multiply again.
80 is the biggest, so the extra subject should go in Group A. That makes sense: an extra subject in A can be paired with every B-and-C pair (4 × 5 = 20 of them), more than any other group gets.

parts.tip: Show all three calculations: "Group A" on its own only gets partial credit.

questions.topic: Arrangements of letters; matching scatterplots to correlation coefficients
questions.fig: Part (b) shows three scatterplots with the same axes. A: points going down from top left to bottom right, close to a straight line. B: points going up from bottom left to top right, close to a straight line. C: points going up but much more spread out.

parts.q: In how many ways can the letters in the word CAMOGIE be arranged?

idea.title: Arrangements and n!
idea.text: To arrange different things in a row, fill the places one at a time. The first place can take any of the items, the next place one fewer, and so on down to 1. 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 is written 7! ("7 factorial").

steps.say: CAMOGIE has 7 letters and they are all different. Think of 7 places to fill, one at a time.
The 1st place can take any of the 7 letters. One is now used, so 6 are left for the 2nd place, then 5 for the 3rd, and so on down to 1.
Multiply. The letters can be arranged in 5040 ways.

parts.tip: Your calculator has a factorial key (x! or n!): 7! = 5040.

parts.q: How many of the arrangements in part (a)(i) start with M and end with a vowel (A, O, I, or E)?

idea.title: Fill the fussy places first
idea.text: When some places have rules, count their options first. Then fill the free places with whatever letters are left, going down by one each time.

steps.say: Fill the places with rules first. The 1st place must be M: only 1 option.
The last place must be a vowel: A, O, I or E. That is 4 options. (M is not a vowel, so putting M first doesn't use up a vowel.)
Two letters are now used, so 5 letters are left for the 5 middle places: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 options.
Multiply. 480 arrangements start with M and end with a vowel.

parts.tip: Always deal with the restricted places (first, last, vowels...) before the free ones.

parts.q: How many arrangements of 3 different letters can be made from the letters in the word CAMOGIE?

steps.say: Now there are only 3 places, but still 7 letters to choose from, with no letter used twice.
Multiply. 210 three-letter arrangements can be made.

parts.q: Three scatterplots are shown below. They are labelled A, B, and C. Each scatterplot has the same axes and scales. The correlation coefficient for each scatterplot was calculated. The results were 0·95, 0·6, and −0·95. Write each of the letters A, B, and C in the correct place in the table below to show which scatterplot corresponds to each correlation coefficient. Use each letter only once.

idea.title: Reading a correlation coefficient
idea.text: r is always between −1 and 1. The sign gives the direction: + means as one goes up, the other goes up; − means as one goes up, the other goes down. The size gives the strength: close to 1 or −1 means the points are close to a straight line; close to 0 means scattered.

steps.say: A goes down from left to right, so it is the negative one: A is −0.95.
B and C both go up, so they are 0.95 and 0.6. B's points sit close to a straight line; C's are spread out. The closer the points are to a line, the nearer r is to 1.
So B is 0.95 and C is 0.6.

parts.q: For scatterplot B, explain why the value you picked is correct.

answer.show: B shows strong positive linear correlation: as x goes up, y goes up, and the points lie close to a straight line, so r is close to 1 (0·95).

parts.scheme: Strong positive linear correlation, so as x goes up y goes up; or the points all lie close to a positive straight line.

steps.say: Say two things: the direction (the points go up, so it's positive) and the strength (they're close to a straight line, so it's strong).
Model answer: B has a strong positive linear correlation: as x goes up, y goes up, and the points all lie close to a straight line, so r is close to 1.
